text: Mexico drug cartel leader's arrest sparks deadly violence in Sinaloa; 11 killed. A major military operation to capture one of the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives triggered a wave of violence in Mexico's northwestern Sinaloa state, leaving at least 11 people dead, authorities said on Saturday. Mexican security forces arrested alleged cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'El Chapo Isidro', following an overnight gun battle with suspected cartel gunmen in the city of Guasave. The violence saw armed men set up roadblocks using burning vehicles, businesses and trucks set ablaze, and residents forced to take shelter as military helicopters and drones flew overhead, reported Associated Press. Mexico's Defense Cabinet said seven suspected cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed in the gun battle during the operation which was carried out with assistance from US intelligence, according to the Mexican government. The violence also disrupted a baseball match in Guasave, where spectators fled the stadium as gunfire rang out. Videos circulating on social media showed people scrambling for cover, burning vehicles and military helicopters flying over the city. ## How the operation unfolded Mexico's Defence Ministry said elite military forces used "stealth and surprise" to establish a security perimeter around the building where Meza Flores was staying. However, suspected cartel operatives retaliated with gunfire and explosives as security forces moved in to arrest him. The group also established at least 10 roadblocks using burning vehicles, delaying the extraction of the arrested leader. Mexican forces were unable to take Meza Flores out of Guasave until around 4 am on Saturday, a federal official told The Associated Press. He was subsequently flown to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors. Local residents described scenes of widespread panic as the fighting spread across the city. Several businesses, including Oxxo convenience stores, were burned, while trucks continued to block roads on Saturday. "The fighting was happening all over Guasave. It spread throughout the city," local journalist Alma Camacho told AP. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch said armed forces would remain deployed across Sinaloa to protect civilians. Read more: How Mexico hunted down FBI's most-wanted drug lord; watch ## Who is 'El Chapo Isidro'? Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known by the nickname 'El Chapo Isidro' is the alleged leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organisation, also known as Los Mazatlecos, a criminal group based in Guasave. He rose through the ranks of the Beltrán Leyva cartel before establishing his own organisation. He is among the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives, with the US agency offering a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest. According to the FBI, Meza Flores was wanted for allegedly possessing, distributing and importing large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States. He was indicted in 2019 on drug trafficking and firearms charges and had also faced drug trafficking charges in 2012. The US Treasury Department had identified his organisation in 2013 as being involved in an extremely violent turf war with the rival Sinaloa Cartel, then led by Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán, who is now serving a prison sentence in the US. Meza Flores was also a key ally of 'Los Mayos', a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel that was designated a foreign terrorist organisation by the Trump administration last year. Meza Flores' arrest comes amid an ongoing power struggle between rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel for control of the northern Mexican state. His organisation has been aligned with Los Mayos, which has been involved in a conflict with another faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. His capture could further intensify the struggle over territory, drug trafficking routes and control of criminal networks. Mexican security analyst David Saucedo warned that targeting senior cartel leaders without dismantling their wider organisations could trigger further violence. The strategy, often called the 'kingpin strategy', focuses on capturing or killing high-ranking cartel figures. However, experts have argued that removing leaders can create power vacuums, prompting rival factions and remaining members to fight for control. "What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said, adding that the arrest of senior figures does not necessarily dismantle the wider network of armed operatives, street-level dealers and political and police connections. The arrest also comes as US President Donald Trump has increased pressure on Mexico to crack down on drug cartels. The Mexican government said intelligence provided by the Trump administration helped authorities locate and capture Meza Flores, although it did not disclose details of the coordination. US and Mexican officials welcomed the arrest. US Ambassador Ronald Johnson said the operation demonstrated what cooperation between the two countries could achieve, while García Harfuch described the detention as "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa". However, analysts have cautioned that the capture of another high-profile cartel leader could set off fresh clashes in a region already grappling with factional violence.
